title.en: Stone pores, grain and weathered edges

summary: Separate mineral-scale texture, visible pits, erosion and deposits so stone detail explains scale and exposure.
objective: Make a weathered stone object readable at both monument and hand-inspection scales.
intent_signals: Make a weathered stone object readable at both monument and hand-inspection scales.
example_prompts: Create a carved stone fountain with coherent shallow pits, softened exposed edges and restrained runoff stains.

principles: Choose a stone and exposure story or state that it is fictional. Generic noise alone does not establish a particular rock type or weathering process.
Use the source as evidence that weathering can affect both volume and appearance; an authored approximation is not the paper's moisture/mineral simulation.
implementation: Separate coarse broken contours, mid-scale pits and fine mineral variation. Put a chip into geometry when it changes the rim or casts a meaningful recess shadow; keep unresolved grain in surface shading.
Align optional stains with the authored runoff/deposit story and interrupts such as ledges, rather than copying one vertical streak onto every orientation.
Compare a broad diffuse view and a raking light close-up at fixed exposure; adjust pore depth and roughness independently so fine grain does not look like uniformly inflated gravel.
observable_checks: At the same world scale, neighboring blocks have compatible grain/pit sizes unless distinct stone is intended.
Silhouette erosion remains visible with textures hidden; color-only weathering does not pretend to remove volume.
An overview retains carved features and mortar boundaries rather than losing them under high-contrast noise.

known_limits: No generic erosion rate, stone age, strength, permeability or wetness-to-friction mapping.
Authored modeling and inspection guidance; no runtime artifact or improvement has been observed for this record.
creative_affordances: Stylized facet groups or painted grain can carry the same hierarchy; pristine or polished stone need not be made porous-looking.

claims.statement: Dorsey and colleagues model weathered stone using moisture and mineral transport within a porous near-surface volume, with erosion changing its surface shape.
claims.scope: Description of the authors' 1999 rendering model, not a prediction for arbitrary stone.
